name: Mira Eyewear
intro: Campaign photography for the launch of Mira's first shield silhouette — a single product, shot as sculpture. One model, one light, and nothing else in the frame.
challenge: Mira was entering eyewear's most crowded season with one product: an oversized shield in gloss black. Every competitor launch that quarter leaned on lifestyle.
solution: We treated the shield as the only black mass in a white void. Front-on symmetry, wet-slicked hair to keep every line vertical, and skin lit to a soft gloss so the matte-black acetate reads as an interruption.
process: Week one was casting and pre-light: we tested four lighting setups against the gloss acetate and kept the simplest, one large frontal source and a white sweep, tuned until the lens reflection read as a clean horizon line instead of studio clutter.
Week two was the shoot: two days in-studio, 41 setups, working through the shot system from widest to tightest.
conclusion: The campaign shipped exactly as shot. No last-minute lifestyle frames, no compromise crops. The shield sold through its first run in five weeks, and the hero image ran unchanged from homepage to out-of-home, which was the original test: one set of pictures strong enough to be the entire launch.

name: NeoYokoto
intro: Naming and full identity for a streetwear label built on the ordinary. A hand-drawn wordmark, a system made to be worn in, and a launch campaign shot in the unglamorous hours the clothes actually live in.
challenge: The founders came to us with garments and no name. What they had instead was a position: streetwear had become costume, styled on rooftops and shot like sneaker ads, and their clothes were meant for the parts of the week nobody photographs.
solution: The name came first. NeoYokoto is an invented place, a district that does not exist, which let the brand build its own mythology instead of borrowing Tokyo's. The wordmark is hand-drawn in marker, kept deliberately uneven, with a small stick figure glyph that works alone as the label's shorthand on tabs, zip pulls, and embroidery.
process: Weeks one and two were naming: 68 candidates, three rounds, trademark screening on the final four. Weeks three to five were the mark itself. We drew roughly 200 wordmark passes by hand, scanned the best 14, and stress-tested them at print scale on actual blanks before choosing.
conclusion: The first drop sold out its hoodie run in eleven days, and the stick figure has already been tattooed on two customers, which is not a metric we planned for but is the only one the founders quote.

name: Meridian Automotive
intro: Launch film and stills for the Meridian x Vettore edition, a limited run of ninety cars. One vehicle, one grey studio, and a campaign built on restraint instead of horsepower theatre.
challenge: Collaboration cars usually get collaboration campaigns: two logos fighting for the hero frame, a mountain road, a drone. Meridian wanted the opposite. Ninety cars would sell themselves; the campaign's job was to make the edition feel inevitable to the ninety people already circling it, and to give both marques imagery they could run under either name.
solution: We shot the car the way we shoot product: seamless grey cove, one enormous soft source, and a near monochrome grade that lets the silver body read as liquid. No location, no motion blur, no badges in the stills. The car's geometry carries every frame, which was the point of the collaboration in the first place.
process: Week one was pre-production: grade tests on paint samples, a full previz of all 22 setups, and a shot order built around the four studio days.

Days one and two were stills, working the cove from full profiles down to macro passes on the lamps and wheels. Days three and four were the film, shot on a motion-control slider so every move could repeat until the reflections behaved.
conclusion: All ninety cars were allocated within a week of the announcement, and the film ran unedited on both brands' channels, which was the quiet test behind the whole brief: one campaign, two masters, zero compromises requested. The stills have since outlived the launch and moved into Vettore's brand book.

name: Pulse Club
intro: Naming, identity, and launch campaign for a gym built on a different question: what if training felt like arriving instead of proving yourself? A brand for people with full schedules who still show up.
challenge: Fitness branding runs on intensity. Condensed type, shouted verbs, before-and-after arithmetic. Pulse Club's founders were building the opposite: a gym where progress means showing up weekly, adjusting the pace, and noticing how each day feels a little different from the last. The identity had to signal effort without aggression and calm without softness.
solution: The name holds the whole position. Pulse is the body's quietest constant, proof of effort that never shouts, and Club reframes membership as belonging rather than subscription.
process: Naming ran the first three weeks: 54 candidates, screened down through two rounds with the founders, trademark checks on the final three.

Weeks four to seven were identity, where the glyph went through 60 drawn passes before the version that read as a pulse at ten meters and a scribble of energy up close. We tested every candidate on a printed shirt before showing it on a screen, because the chest print was always going to be the brand's real home.
conclusion: Pulse Club opened with 300 founding memberships gone before the doors did, and the first merch run sold out to people who had never set foot in the gym, which says the identity works as belonging before it works as marketing. The in-house team has run the system solo since week one.

name: Basalt
intro: Campaign photography for Basalt's winter collection, starring the actor Solitaire. One figure, one landscape of black sand, and a collection shot as choreography instead of catalogue.
challenge: Casting a famous face is usually a shortcut, and that was the risk. Solitaire's presence could carry the campaign so easily that the clothes would become costume in someone else's story. Basalt wanted the opposite hierarchy: the collection first, the landscape second, the fame a distant third.
solution: We built the campaign on movement rather than portraiture. Working with a movement director, we developed a sequence of held, sculptural poses that turn the body into a form the garments drape and break across. The face appears, but rarely straight on, and the ash dusting and hard side light push it toward sculpture.
process: Weeks one and two were preparation: location scout and permits, garment tests against the sand in matching light, and two rehearsal days with the movement director and a stand-in, building a shot list of 18 held poses timed to the minute.
The ash treatment was tested on set stand-ins until it read as mineral rather than makeup.
conclusion: The collection shipped with a single image system across lookbook, store windows and social, and the silhouette-first frames became the season's most-saved posts. You recognize the clothes first and the actor second, which was the whole brief.

name: Kano
intro: Naming and identity for a flower studio that treats arrangements as sculpture. A hand-drawn mark, monochrome botanical photography, and a brand that lets the flowers be the only color in the room.
challenge: Flower branding defaults to prettiness: pastel palettes, script fonts, watercolor everything. Kano's founder trained in ikebana and builds arrangements closer to sculpture than bouquet, sold to restaurants, hotels, and galleries rather than weddings. The identity had to read as an art practice with a delivery van, not a florist with ambitions.
solution: The name is short, planted, and slightly unfamiliar, and the wordmark is drawn by hand until the letters moved like stems, with a bloom glyph sprouting from the K that works alone as the studio's stamp on wrap, ribbon, and cards. The mark carries all the softness the brand will ever need, which freed everything else to be severe.
process: Naming took the first two weeks: 40 candidates pushed through sound and meaning checks across the studio's three client languages.
Weeks three and four were the mark, roughly 120 drawn passes, then the bloom glyph separated out and tested at stamp size on kraft wrap before anything went digital.
conclusion: Kano rebranded on a Monday and had its first gallery commission by that Friday, from a curator who said the Instagram grid looked like an exhibition. Walk-in trade held steady, which was the balance the whole brief hinged on.

name: Russells
intro: Naming, identity, and an own-label packaging line for a dog store and grooming studio that refuses to be cute. A geometric hound, a concrete flagship, and a brand built for the humans who take their dogs seriously.
challenge: Pet retail is drowning in paw prints, pastels, and puns. Russells was opening a flagship store and grooming studio in a neighborhood of design-literate owners, selling considered gear and its own food and treat line. The founders wanted a brand their customers would respect as much as the studios and cafes next door, without tipping into coldness.
solution: The name came from the shop dog, a Jack Russell, and it gave the brand a family surname's confidence: Russells, like a business that has been on this corner for decades. The mark is a hound's head built from hard angles, an X for an eye and diamonds for teeth, fierce at first glance and a grin at the second.
process: Weeks one and two settled the name and registered it without drama. The mark took four weeks and roughly 90 passes, most of them spent tuning how sharp the teeth could be before the grin disappeared.
We tested at three scales throughout: facade, package, and stamp, because a mark that only works at one size is a logo, not an identity.
conclusion: Russells opened to a queue with dogs in it, and the own-label treat line became the store's best seller within the first month. The sign is now a local landmark and has its own geotag, which no one planned and no one is complaining about.

name: Studio 116
intro: Identity for an interior architecture practice in Luxembourg, dedicated to residential spaces defined by simplicity, material honesty, and thoughtful spatial composition — extending the studio's architectural philosophy into a cohesive visual language.
challenge: The challenge was a brand identity that captured Studio 116's refined architectural approach while staying versatile across physical and digital applications: understated yet distinctive, translating restraint, precision, and material sensitivity into a visual system.
solution: A minimal, responsive identity inspired by architectural principles. A restrained palette of neutral tones, dark accents, and clean typography creates a calm yet confident presence, and a flexible naming system — from "Studio116" to "S116" — lets the identity adapt naturally to different formats.
process: The process began with Studio 116's philosophy of creating refined residential environments through simplicity and material awareness. That informed a visual system centered on contrast, rhythm, and editorial precision, with typography as the foundation, supported by a muted palette and carefully balanced compositions.
conclusion: The final identity positions Studio 116 as a contemporary practice that values clarity, craftsmanship, and enduring design. Rather than competing for attention, the system communicates confidence through restraint — a natural extension of the spaces the studio creates.
